blocks.text: In the last lesson a vector was just a list of numbers sitting in order. That is true, but it misses the reason vectors are so useful in AI. This lesson shows you what a vector actually means, because that meaning is the entire idea behind how embeddings and semantic search work.

blocks.alt: A vector shown as both a point in space and an arrow from the origin
blocks.caption: The two ways of thinking about a vector covered in this lesson.

blocks.text: 1. A Vector Is a Point, and Also an Arrow
Take the vector [4, 3]. There are two equally valid ways to picture it, and both are useful at different times.

items: As a point: go 4 steps along the x-axis, then 3 steps up the y-axis, and mark that exact spot.
As an arrow: starting from the origin, the point (0, 0), draw a straight line to that same spot. The arrow has both a length and a direction.

blocks.alt: A vector (4, 3) drawn as an arrow from the origin, with dashed lines showing 4 steps along x and 3 steps up y
blocks.caption: The same two numbers, [4, 3], drawn as a point and as an arrow from the origin.

blocks.text: The dashed lines in the picture show exactly where the two numbers come from: the vector reaches 4 units to the right and 3 units up. Nothing about the arrow is mysterious, it is simply a visual summary of the same two numbers you already had in the list.
1.1 The Same Vector Can Start Anywhere

So far every arrow has started at the origin, which is called a position vector, since it doubles as a way of describing a fixed point. But a vector on its own only really carries two pieces of information, a length and a direction, and that same length and direction can be drawn starting from anywhere, not only the origin.

blocks.alt: The same vector, 2 right and 1 up, drawn once from the origin and once starting from a different point
blocks.caption: Both arrows are the exact same vector, they just start in different places.

blocks.text: This distinction matters once vectors start representing movement or change rather than a fixed location, for example how much a recommendation score shifted after a new rating, which is a change, not a position, and can sensibly be drawn starting from wherever the previous score happened to be.

Most of the diagrams in this lesson still draw vectors from the origin anyway, since that is the simplest way to talk about a single fixed embedding. Just keep in mind that the origin-starting picture is a convenient default, not a hard rule the vector itself is obeying.
2. Reading Off the Components

Each number inside a vector is called a component, and it tells you how far to move along one specific axis. The first number is the x-component, the second is the y-component, and so on for however many dimensions the vector has.

This is exactly why order matters so much for a vector, mentioned back in the first lesson. Swap the two numbers to [3, 4] and you get a completely different arrow, pointing to a different spot, even though it is made of the same two numbers.
2.1 Coordinate Systems Are a Choice

The origin and the direction of each axis are a convention someone picked, not a fact handed down by nature. Two different embedding models can place the word "cat" at two completely different sets of coordinates, and both can be entirely correct.

blocks.title: What actually stays meaningful
blocks.content: The absolute coordinates a model assigns are not meant to be compared across different models. What matters, and what stays meaningful, is the relative distance between points produced by the same model, "cat" sitting closer to "dog" than to "car" is the part that carries real information, not the specific numbers themselves.

blocks.text: This is also why you cannot mix embeddings from two different models in the same search or comparison and expect a sensible result. Even if both models happen to output vectors of the same length, their coordinate systems were learned independently and have no shared meaning between them.
3. A 3D Example You Already Know

Before jumping to hundreds of dimensions, it helps to see one more dimension added to something familiar. A color on a screen is usually stored as three numbers, red, green, and blue, each between 0 and 255. That is a 3-dimensional vector you have almost certainly used without ever calling it one.

code.content:
red = (255, 0, 0)     # a 3-D vector: full red, no green, no blue
purple = (128, 0, 128) # a 3-D vector: half red, no green, half blue

blocks.text: Picturing this one takes three axes instead of two, red-axis, green-axis, blue-axis, but the idea is identical to the 2D arrow from the last section: each of the three numbers says how far to move along one specific axis. Nothing new had to be invented to go from 2 dimensions to 3.
3.1 Picturing Three Dimensions
A third axis can still be drawn on a flat page by angling it so it looks like it is coming toward you, the same trick used in most textbook sketches of 3D space.

blocks.alt: Three axes, x, y, and z, drawn from a common origin at different angles, with one vector arrow pointing to the point (2, 3, 1)
blocks.caption: A flat page cannot truly show depth, but angling the third axis is enough to build the right intuition.

blocks.text: The vector (2, 3, 1) in the picture above means exactly what you would expect by now: move 2 along x, 3 along y, and 1 along z, then draw the arrow from the origin to wherever that lands.

Beyond 3 dimensions, even this angled-axis trick stops working, since there is no way to angle a fourth line so it looks visually distinct from the other three. This is precisely the wall every visualization of high-dimensional embeddings eventually runs into, and it is exactly why dimensionality reduction techniques exist, to flatten a high-dimensional cloud of points down to 2 or 3 dimensions that can actually be plotted, at the cost of losing some detail in the process.
4. From 2D to Many Dimensions
Real AI vectors are almost never 2 or 3 dimensional. A typical word or sentence embedding might have 384, 768, or even a few thousand dimensions.

blocks.title: You cannot draw it, but the idea still holds
blocks.content: Nobody can sketch 768 axes on paper, and you do not need to. The exact same idea from the 2D and 3D pictures above still applies: each of those 768 numbers tells you how far to move along one of 768 directions. The arrow-from-the-origin intuition transfers perfectly, even though drawing it directly is impossible past 3 dimensions.

blocks.text: It can help to think of each additional dimension as one more independent question being asked about the thing being represented. A word embedding with 768 dimensions is, loosely speaking, the answer to 768 different learned questions about that word, all at once, packed into a single point in space.
5. Why This Geometric View Matters for AI

This point-in-space idea is not just a neat way to visualize numbers, it is the actual foundation embeddings are built on. An embedding model turns something meaningful, a word, a sentence, an image, into a vector, specifically so that similar things end up as nearby points, and different things end up far apart.

The word "king" and the word "queen" end up as two points sitting close together in embedding space, because they are used in similar ways. The word "king" and the word "banana" end up far apart, because they almost never mean or relate to the same thing. Nobody hand-picks these positions, a model learns them from data, but the geometric idea, meaning as distance, is exactly what you just saw with a simple 2D arrow.

items: Semantic search: finding documents whose embeddings sit close to a query embedding.
Recommendation systems: finding items whose embeddings sit close to a user preference embedding.
Retrieval for RAG pipelines: finding the chunks of text whose embeddings sit closest to a question.
Clustering: grouping points that naturally sit close together in the same region of space.

blocks.text: 5.1 Seeing It as a Pipeline
Stitched together, the last few sections describe a real, working pipeline used constantly in production AI systems.

blocks.alt: A pipeline diagram: a word or sentence goes into an embedding model, comes out as a vector, and gets compared by distance to find its nearest neighbors
blocks.caption: This exact pipeline, text in, vector out, distance compared, is the engine behind search, recommendations, and RAG retrieval.

blocks.text: 5.2 Common Real-World Vector Sizes
To make the "hundreds or thousands of dimensions" claim from earlier concrete, here are dimension counts from embedding models you are likely to actually encounter.

blocks.content: {"headers":["Model family","Typical dimensions"],"rows":[["Older word embeddings (word2vec, GloVe)","100 to 300"],["Small sentence embedding models","384"],["BERT-base style models","768"],["Large modern text embedding APIs","1536 to 3072"]]}

blocks.text: Bigger is not automatically better here either. A larger embedding can capture more nuance, but it also costs more memory to store and more compute to compare, which is a real engineering trade-off covered properly in the cost versus performance corners of system design, not just a math detail.
6. The Gap Between Two Vectors Is Also a Vector

If two vectors are both points in the same space, the straight line connecting them describes something meaningful too: subtracting one from the other gives a new vector that points from one to the other. This single idea is what the upcoming distance and similarity lessons are built on.

code.content:
a = [4, 3]
b = [1, 5]
difference = [a[0] - b[0], a[1] - b[1]]
print(difference)   # [3, -2]

blocks.alt: Vectors A and B drawn from the origin, with a dashed grey arrow connecting the tip of B to the tip of A, labeled A minus B
blocks.caption: The dashed arrow is the vector A minus B, it points from B directly to A.

blocks.text: That gap vector, A minus B, has its own magnitude, and that magnitude is exactly the straight-line distance between points A and B. This is worth sitting with for a moment: distance between two things is nothing more than the length of the vector that connects them.
6.1 Many Points at Once: A Cloud of Meaning
Real embedding spaces hold far more than two points at a time, often millions. Plotting several word embeddings together shows the clustering effect directly rather than just describing it.

blocks.alt: A scatter of points representing word embeddings, with animal words clustered together in blue, vehicle words clustered together in red, and unrelated words sitting apart in grey
blocks.caption: Related words land near each other with no one manually placing them there, the model learned this arrangement from data.

blocks.text: Nobody instructed the model to put animal words in one region and vehicle words in another. That clustering falls directly out of training on real language, where those words tend to appear in similar contexts.
6.2 Clusters Are Not Officially Labeled

It is worth being precise about what the picture above actually shows. The model was never told the words animals or vehicles as category names, those labels were added afterward, by a person looking at the result, to describe a grouping that emerged naturally from the numbers. The vectors themselves are just coordinates, the meaningful clusters are something a human, or a separate clustering algorithm, recognizes afterward.
7. A Worked Example: Comparing Two Vectors

Say you have two very short profiles, each turned into a 2-dimensional vector for the sake of a simple example: profile A is [4, 3] and profile B is [1, 5]. Plotting both as arrows from the same origin makes it easy to compare them visually before doing any actual math.

blocks.alt: Two vectors, A at (4, 3) in blue and B at (1, 5) in red, both drawn as arrows from the same origin
blocks.caption: Two vectors plotted from the same origin. Just from the picture, you can already see they point in noticeably different directions.

blocks.text: Just by looking at the picture, you can already tell these two arrows point in fairly different directions, one leans more to the right, the other leans more steeply upward. That visual difference in direction is the entire intuition behind measuring how similar two things are, which is exactly what the next lessons on magnitude and distance build on directly.

blocks.content: {"headers":["Vector","Components","Plain description"],"rows":[["A","(4, 3)","Mostly to the right, a little bit up"],["B","(1, 5)","Mostly upward, only a little to the right"]]}

blocks.text: 7.1 Extending to Three Vectors
Add a third profile, C at (3, 1), to the same picture as A and B from before.

blocks.alt: Three vectors, A, B, and C, all drawn as arrows from the same origin, pointing in three different directions
blocks.caption: With three vectors on the same picture, you can start comparing every pair, not just one.

blocks.text: Looking at the picture, C sits at a shallower angle than A, leaning further toward the x-axis, while B leans steeply toward the y-axis. Purely from this picture, C looks closer in direction to A than B does, a judgment the next lessons on magnitude and similarity will turn into an exact number instead of a visual guess.

Nothing stops this from extending further, to four, five, or thousands of vectors compared at once, which is exactly what a real similarity search does under the hood: the same pairwise comparison shown here with three vectors, just run against every stored vector instead of two.
8. Common Mistakes

items: Assuming a vector has to be 2 or 3 dimensional to "count" as a real vector, most AI vectors have hundreds or thousands of dimensions.
Mixing up the order of subtraction, A minus B points from B to A, while B minus A points the opposite way, from A to B.
Thinking two vectors that look different as lists cannot be close together in space, direction and distance are what matter, not how the numbers happen to be written.
Comparing raw coordinates from two different embedding models as if they share the same coordinate system, they almost never do.

blocks.text: A closely related mistake worth calling out on its own: treating the components of two different vectors as directly comparable one by one, like assuming the third number in vector A means the same thing as the third number in vector B. Inside a single, consistent embedding model this is fine, but it breaks down the moment the two vectors come from different sources.
9. Where These Vectors Actually Live

Once text, images, or audio get turned into embeddings, those vectors have to be stored somewhere and searched quickly. Purpose-built vector databases exist specifically for this: given a query vector, find the nearest stored vectors out of millions or billions, in a fraction of a second.

blocks.title: A preview of what is coming
blocks.content: How a database finds the nearest points that quickly, without checking every single one, is its own topic covered later in this module under approximate nearest neighbor search. For now, the important part is simply knowing that embeddings do not just sit in a spreadsheet, they get placed into a system built entirely around this geometric point-in-space idea.

blocks.text: It is worth remembering that a vector database is still, underneath everything, just storing lists of numbers and running the same distance calculations covered in this module. The engineering challenge is entirely about doing that at massive scale and speed, not about inventing new math beyond what a vector, its magnitude, and the gap between two vectors already describe.
9.1 Practice: Which Vector Is Closer
Given vector A at (4, 3), which of the following two vectors would you expect to sit closer to it in space, just by picturing the arrows: X at (5, 4), or Y at (0, 6)?

blocks.title: Answer
blocks.content: X at (5, 4) sits much closer to A. It points in almost the same direction and almost the same length, just a small nudge away. Y at (0, 6) points in a very different direction, almost straight up rather than diagonally, and lands noticeably farther from A. The exact distance calculation is covered properly once the magnitude lesson introduces how to measure it precisely, but the visual instinct here is already the correct one.

blocks.text: This kind of quick visual estimate is a genuinely useful habit to build, since it gives you a sanity check against the exact numeric answer a similarity calculation returns later. If the number disagrees wildly with what the picture suggests, that mismatch is usually worth investigating rather than trusting the number blindly.
Key Takeaway

A vector can be read two ways at once, as a point in space, or as an arrow from the origin to that point, and both are exactly the same thing. Each component of the vector says how far to move along one axis, which is why the order of the numbers changes what the vector actually points to.

Real AI embeddings live in hundreds or thousands of dimensions, far more than anyone can draw on paper, but the same arrow-from-the-origin intuition still applies exactly. That geometric view is the whole idea behind embeddings in the first place: similar things end up as nearby points, and different things end up as distant points, with the gap between any two points being, itself, just another vector.
